logline: The Fisher family runs a Los Angeles funeral home where every episode opens with a death - and every season maps how grief, desire, and mortality run through the living as much as the dead.

renewal.note: Five-season run on HBO concluded August 21, 2005. Creator Alan Ball confirmed the finale as the intended ending. The series finale is widely cited as the greatest in television history.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 scored 90% on Rotten Tomatoes and a Metacritic of 74. Critics called it unlike anything HBO had produced: a comedy-drama about death that was simultaneously hilarious, surreal, and bracingly honest about grief.

pull_quotes.text: Six Feet Under establishes from the start that it will be unflinching and brazen and, as it happens, scorchingly brilliant.
So daring, richly multi-dimensional and culturally provocative that it's almost anti-television.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 premiered June 2001 and immediately positioned itself as something HBO had not produced before: a drama where death is not dramatic punctuation but the condition through which every episode is filtered. The Rotten Tomatoes score of 90% and a Metacritic of 74 reflected critical consensus that Alan Ball had found a format - the cold open death, the Fisher family response, the surreal grief hallucinations - that was formally inventive rather than just macabre. The Washington Post called it 'scorchingly brilliant.' The Baltimore Sun called it 'almost anti-television.' Peter Krause and Michael C. Hall were singled out as a sibling pair whose chemistry carried the show's emotional weight.

episode_reviews.title: Pilot
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series premiere establishes the Fisher family's loss and the funeral home world with economy and black humour. The format - cold open death, then the family's professional and personal response - is introduced with confidence. Nate's arrival back in Los Angeles sets the show's central dynamic between the person who left and the family that stayed.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Nathaniel Fisher Sr.'s first appearance as a ghost - the show's surrealist register introduced without apology.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 scored 79% on Rotten Tomatoes as critics found the show's middle period less focused than its debut, though individual performances - particularly Rachel Griffiths and Lauren Ambrose - continued to draw consistent praise.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 has a 79-percent Rotten Tomatoes score, and the writing continues to balance ensemble ambitions with a central narrative drive. The Nate-Brenda relationship, the David-Keith dynamic, and Ruth's new romantic life give the season multiple competing threads that can feel occasionally diffuse. Individual performances stay sharply defined: Rachel Griffiths's Brenda is among television's most complex female characters of the period. The season's dark humour remains as precise as the debut, with the funeral home serving as a comic chamber of absurdity as reliably as ever.
seasons.season_over_season: The show expands its ensemble with confidence but the central arc proves less focused than the debut year.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 recovered to 90% on Rotten Tomatoes. The Nate health arc and Claire's art school arc gave the season structural clarity, and critics called this the year the ensemble finally cohered around a shared thematic question about how people choose to live.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 returned to a 90% on Rotten Tomatoes as the ensemble landed with greater structural clarity. The Nate AVM storyline introduced mortality as something happening to the Fishers rather than merely around them, and the Claire art school arc opened the show’s generational canvas with strong thematic pull. Lauren Ambrose’s Claire emerged as the show’s moral centre, the character most willing to interrogate what the family represents. The Dallas Morning News described the show as “seldom less than bracingly original,” a verdict that held through the season’s best hours.
seasons.season_over_season: The ensemble achieves its first full coherence; mortality arrives inside the family rather than just as professional backdrop.

bollymeter.basis: Season 4 dropped to 50% on Rotten Tomatoes - the series' critical low. Critics found the Nate-Maggie storyline and the Brenda pregnancy arc diffuse, and the season's structural problems were more visible than at any other point in the run.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 registers a 50% critical low on Rotten Tomatoes. The year spreads the series' characteristic strengths, including character specificity, tonal command, and ensemble chemistry, across storylines that feel like structural padding. The Nate-Maggie affair and how it handles the Brenda relationship diffuse the character arcs, pulling them toward regression. Individual scenes and performances continue to meet the show's standard, but the season as a whole stands out as the moment in Six Feet Under's run where the format's demands outrun the writers' solutions.
seasons.season_over_season: The show's acknowledged trough - critical consensus identified structural drift that the final season's creative regrouping would need to correct.

bollymeter.basis: Season 5 scored 97% on Rotten Tomatoes and produced the finale 'Everyone's Waiting,' which is cited by critics and audiences - including George R.R. Martin to Variety - as the greatest television finale ever made. The seven-minute closing montage set to Sia's 'Breathe Me' is a consensus landmark.

seasons.review_body: Season 5 concluded Six Feet Under with a Rotten Tomatoes score of 97 percent and features what stands as one of the medium's greatest television finales. The final episode, "Everyone's Waiting," ends with a seven-minute montage: Claire driving east as Sia's "Breathe Me" plays, followed by the futures of every major character in rapid, accumulating flashes across decades. The sequence lands as an especially emotionally devastating run of television drama, combining grief, momentum, and craft in a tightly structured crescendo. The season and series end as proof that American television can deliver genuine formal and emotional art.
seasons.season_over_season: A complete recovery and the show’s finest year: the finale’s seven-minute montage stands as the single greatest scene in prestige television history.

episode_reviews.title: Everyone's Waiting
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale sends Claire to New York and then - in its final seven minutes - shows every Fisher's future across decades, each death arriving with the same matter-of-factness the show applied to strangers in its cold opens. The sequence achieves something rare in television: the formal and emotional simultaneously at full extension.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Claire's drive east and the montage that follows - the most discussed closing sequence in prestige drama, and the one most often called the medium's finest achievement.

critic_note.text: That last episode was far and away the best finale in the entire history of television, and I cannot imagine how anyone could possibly do better.
